index.html.title: Overview
index.html.summary: Overview Addax is a high-throughput, forward-only framework for reading and writing tabular data in delimiter-separated formats of any dialect. The data model follows the W3C recommendation Model for Tabular Data and Metadata on the Web (2015). Typed values are read and written in fixed, culture-independent formats based on W3C CSVW, ISO 8601-1:2019, RFC 3987, RFC 4648 and RFC 9562. The library has two APIs. The high-level API consists of TabularReader<T> and TabularWriter<T>. They read or write one record per call and delegate the mapping between a record and a .NET object to a record handler, generated at compile time from attributes or written by hand. The low-level API consists of TabularReader and TabularWriter, on which the high-level API is built. They move forward through a stream one field at a time and read or write each field as a string, as a character sequence, or as a typed value. High-level API should be used when the records have a fixed structure that maps to a custom type, with or without a header, comments are only skipped, and each record is used as a whole. Low-level API should be used when the structure varies or is known only at run time, the stream contains comments to process, only some fields are needed, or a field is processed without creating a string. The library and its source generator ship together in the Addax.Formats.Tabular NuGet package. Every reader and writer needs a TabularDialect, which defines the line terminator, the delimiter and the quote character, and optionally a separate escape character and a comment prefix. The examples use the RFC 4180 dialect: records end with CRLF, fields are separated by commas, and fields that need it are enclosed in double quotes. Both examples write the same two books to a file and read them back, first with the high-level API and then with the low-level API. Examples: High-level API The source generator creates a record handler at compile time that maps the members of the type to fields. Write the records to a file, then read them back one record at a time. The writer writes one record per TabularWriter<T>.WriteRecord() call, and the reader moves to each record and returns it as a Book: var books = new Book[] { new("Lewis Carroll", "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland", new(1865, 11, 9)), new("H. G. Wells", "The Time Machine", new(1895, 5, 7)) }; var dialect = new TabularDialect("\r\n", ',', '"'); using (var stream = File.Create("books.csv")) using (var writer = new TabularWriter<Book>(stream, dialect)) { foreach (var book in books) { writer.WriteRecord(book); } } using (var stream = File.OpenRead("books.csv")) using (var reader = new TabularReader<Book>(stream, dialect)) { while (reader.TryReadRecord()) { var book = reader.CurrentRecord; Console.WriteLine($"{book.Author}: {book.Title} ({book.Published})"); } } [TabularRecord] internal record Book( [property: TabularFieldOrder(0)] string Author, [property: TabularFieldOrder(1)] string Title, [property: TabularFieldOrder(2)] DateOnly Published); Examples: Low-level API The same file, written and read one field at a time. The writer writes fields until TabularWriter.WriteEndOfRecord() ends the record, and the reader moves to each record and reads its fields in order: var books = new[] { new Book("Lewis Carroll", "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland", new(1865, 11, 9)), new Book("H. G. Wells", "The Time Machine", new(1895, 5, 7)) }; var dialect = new TabularDialect("\r\n", ',', '"'); using (var stream = File.Create("books.csv")) using (var writer = new TabularWriter(stream, dialect)) { foreach (var book in books) { writer.WriteString(book.Author); writer.WriteString(book.Title); writer.WriteDateOnly(book.Published); writer.WriteEndOfRecord(); } } using (var stream = File.OpenRead("books.csv")) using (var reader = new TabularReader(stream, dialect)) { while (reader.TryMoveToNextRecord()) { reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetString(out var bookAuthor); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetString(out var bookTitle); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetDateOnly(out var bookPublished); Console.WriteLine($"{bookAuthor}: {bookTitle} ({bookPublished})"); } }

Integers are read within the range of the type, and System.Numerics.BigInteger has no range limit. A System.TimeSpan is read with an optional leading "-", and any of its components may be omitted as long as one remains, together with T when no time component remains, and a component may exceed its carry range, as in PT36H. A negative value is written with a leading "-". A System.DateTime read with a zone is converted to UTC and has UTC kind, and one read without a zone has unspecified kind. A System.DateTimeOffset read without a zone has the offset +00:00. System.DateOnly and System.TimeOnly ignore the zone. A System.Uri is read as an absolute or relative URI reference, and is written in its escaped form when it is absolute and as its original string when it is relative. Hexadecimal digits are read in any case and written in lowercase. A Base64 value is read and written with padding, and white space inside it is ignored when it is read. An empty field reads as no bytes, and no bytes and null are written as an empty field. Binary data has no default form: the accessor, the write method or the converter names the encoding. Options Readers and writers of both APIs take a TabularOptions instance, and three of its options change how field values are read and written. TrimWhitespace With TabularOptions.TrimWhitespace set to true, the reader trims every field after decoding, so the quoted field " Alice " reads as "Alice" and a field of only white space reads as an empty field, and the converters receive the trimmed field. The writer trims every value and comment before quoting it. FormatProvider Readers and writers pass the converters a format provider, which is the invariant culture unless TabularOptions.FormatProvider sets another one, and the format provider affects only: Numbers: the sign symbols, the decimal separator, and the symbols of infinity and NaN. Dates and times with a custom format: the names of months and days, the separators and the calendar. StringFactory Readers create the strings of fields through TabularOptions.StringFactory. A TabularStringFactory created with a maximum length pools strings: a field of at most that length returns the pooled string instance for the same characters. The pool holds a fixed number of strings, 4,096 by default, where a new string replaces the pooled string it collides with, so it suits fields with few distinct values that repeat, such as codes, categories or names: using var factory = new TabularStringFactory(maxLength: 32); var dialect = new TabularDialect("\r\n", ',', '"'); var options = new TabularOptions { StringFactory = factory }; using var stream = File.OpenRead("books.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader(stream, dialect, options); By default, the strings behind URIs are not pooled, because the built-in Uri converter does not use the option. A TabularUriConverter created with the factory pools them when it replaces the built-in converter, whether it is stored in the options or the registry, passed to TryGet, Get and Write, or named in a [TabularConverter<T>] attribute through a derived class. Standards The BNF grammar follows section 8, "Parsing Tabular Data", of the W3C recommendation "Model for Tabular Data and Metadata on the Web". RFC 4180 corresponds to the dialect { "\r\n", ',', '"' }. The reader also accepts any Unicode characters in fields, a lone CR or LF in an unquoted field, and records with different numbers of fields. The CSVW dialect description maps to the library as follows: CSVW Addax Purpose commentPrefix TabularDialect.CommentPrefix The character that starts a comment record, if the dialect has comment records. delimiter TabularDialect.Delimiter The character that separates the fields of a value record. doubleQuote TabularDialect.EscapeChar Whether a quote character is escaped by doubling it. encoding TabularOptions.Encoding The encoding of the stream (UTF-8 by default). lineTerminators TabularDialect.LineTerminator The single sequence of one or two characters that ends a record. quoteChar TabularDialect.QuoteChar The character that encloses a quoted field, which every dialect requires. trim TabularOptions.TrimWhitespace Whether field values are trimmed, at both ends, of the whitespace characters. References ISO 8601-1:2019, Date and time, Part 1: Basic rules RFC 3987, Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs) RFC 4180, Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files RFC 4648, The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings RFC 9562, Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs) W3C, Model for Tabular Data and Metadata on the Web W3C, Metadata Vocabulary for Tabular Data

topics/high-level-api.html.title: High-level API
topics/high-level-api.html.summary:
High-level API TabularReader<T> reads each value record of a stream as a T, and TabularWriter<T> writes each T as a record, through a record handler. Both take the same stream, dialect and options as the low-level API, and every member that reads or writes has an asynchronous counterpart with a cancellation token, for example TryReadRecordAsync for TryReadRecord. A record handler, a TabularHandler<T>, converts between one record and one T. The constructor of the reader or writer selects it once: The entry for typeof(T) in TabularOptions.Handlers of the options. Otherwise the entry for typeof(T) in TabularRegistry.Handlers. Otherwise the constructor throws an InvalidOperationException. The registry holds the built-in array handlers, the handlers generated for [TabularRecord] types, and any handler stored in it. A reader or writer keeps the handler it selected, so later changes to the registry do not affect it. Reading records TryReadRecord reads the next value record into CurrentRecord, and TrySkipRecord moves past it without calling the handler. Both skip comment records. CurrentRecordRef returns a read-only reference to the record instead of a copy. The samples read and write observations.csv: city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.OpenRead("observations.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader<Observation>(stream, dialect); while (reader.TryReadRecord()) { var observation = reader.CurrentRecord; Console.WriteLine($"{observation.City}: {observation.Temperature}"); } [TabularRecord] internal record Observation( [property: TabularFieldOrder(0), TabularFieldName("city")] string City, [property: TabularFieldOrder(1), TabularFieldName("lat")] double Latitude, [property: TabularFieldOrder(2), TabularFieldName("lon")] double Longitude, [property: TabularFieldOrder(3), TabularFieldName("date")] DateOnly Date, [property: TabularFieldOrder(4), TabularFieldName("temperature")] double Temperature); When the handler's Header is not null, the first value record of the stream is the header, and the first TryReadRecord or TrySkipRecord skips it. The header is identified by position only: its fields are not compared with the names in Header, and fields map to members by their order. An exception from the handler leaves the reader usable, and the next call continues with the next record. This includes the TabularException that the generated and array handlers throw for a missing field or a field that cannot be converted. A failure of the field reader underneath faults the reader. Writing records WriteRecord writes one record. When the handler's Header is not null, the writer writes the header before the first record, or on disposal when no record was written. The writer buffers and flushes like the low-level writer. The sample writes observations.csv with the Observation type: var observations = new Observation[] { new("Kyiv", 50.4501, 30.5234, new(2024, 2, 3), -2.5), new("Ottawa", 45.4215, -75.6972, new(2024, 2, 3), -11.5) }; var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.Create("observations.csv"); using var writer = new TabularWriter<Observation>(stream, dialect); foreach (var observation in observations) { writer.WriteRecord(observation); } [TabularRecord] internal record Observation( [property: TabularFieldOrder(0), TabularFieldName("city")] string City, [property: TabularFieldOrder(1), TabularFieldName("lat")] double Latitude, [property: TabularFieldOrder(2), TabularFieldName("lon")] double Longitude, [property: TabularFieldOrder(3), TabularFieldName("date")] DateOnly Date, [property: TabularFieldOrder(4), TabularFieldName("temperature")] double Temperature); city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 Any exception from WriteRecord or Flush faults the writer: every further call throws an InvalidOperationException, and disposal writes no header. The fields that a failed handler had written stay in the output as a record. Generated record handlers For every class, struct, record class and record struct marked with TabularRecordAttribute, the source generator creates a record handler at compile time, with no reflection at run time. A module initializer of the assembly that declares the type stores the handler in TabularRegistry.Handlers, so every reader and writer for the type finds it. Types the generator cannot map are reported with generator diagnostics. Attribute Target Effect [TabularRecord] class, struct Generates a record handler for the type. [TabularFieldOrder(n)] field, property Maps the member to the field at the zero-based position n of the record. [TabularFieldName("name")] field, property Gives the field a name, used in the header. [TabularConverter<TConverter>] field, property Converts the member's values with TConverter. [assembly: TabularConverter<TConverter>] assembly Converts every value of the type that TConverter converts with TConverter, in every mapped member of the assembly without a converter attribute of its own. Only a member with TabularFieldOrderAttribute is mapped: a field or a property, declared or inherited, that is accessible from any code of the assembly that declares the record type. The handler reads a field into a member it can set, including through an init accessor, and writes a field from a member it can get. A generated handler supports reading when the type is not abstract, at least one mapped member can be set, and the handler can construct the type in one of two ways: With a parameterless constructor and an object initializer, so init accessors and required members are supported. Every required member must be a mapped member that can be set. The implicit parameterless constructor of a struct counts only when the struct declares no constructor with parameters. Otherwise, with the primary constructor of a positional record. Every parameter is mapped with [property: TabularFieldOrder(n)], every mapped member that can be set is such a parameter, the parameters have no modifiers or default values, and the type declares no required members. It supports writing when at least one mapped member can be read and the orders of these members are 0, 1, …, n−1, without gaps. Otherwise TryReadRecord or WriteRecord throws a NotSupportedException. On read, the handler reads the fields of the members that can be set, in field order, and skips the other fields before the last of them. Fields after the last one are ignored. A missing field or a field that cannot be converted throws a TabularException that names the record, the field and the member. A generated handler has a header when at least one mapped member has [TabularFieldName]. The header has one name for every field order from 0 to the highest mapped order, with an empty name for an unnamed member and for an order without a member. For the Observation type with names only on City and Temperature, the header is city,,,,temperature: [TabularRecord] internal record Observation( [property: TabularFieldOrder(0), TabularFieldName("city")] string City, [property: TabularFieldOrder(1)] double Latitude, [property: TabularFieldOrder(2)] double Longitude, [property: TabularFieldOrder(3)] DateOnly Date, [property: TabularFieldOrder(4), TabularFieldName("temperature")] double Temperature); The values of a mapped member are converted with the first of: The converter named by the member's [TabularConverter<TConverter>] attribute. The converter named by an [assembly: TabularConverter<TConverter>] attribute for the member type, or for T of a Nullable<T> member. The converter that the reader or writer resolves for the type, as described in Value converters. A converter named by an attribute is chosen at compile time, and the handler creates one instance of it per member. It must derive from TabularConverter<T> for the member type and have a public parameterless constructor. A member of a type without a built-in converter, including enumerations and byte[], needs a converter from an attribute, the options or the registry. Empty fields and null depend on the member type: Member type Empty field on read null on write Nullable<T>, for example int? null empty field nullable reference type, for example string?, Uri?, byte[]? null passed to the converter, and the built-in converters write an empty field string empty string empty field any other type passed to the converter, which rejects it for most value types with a TabularException Custom record handlers A custom handler derives from TabularHandler<T> and overrides the members it supports, since Read, ReadAsync, Write and WriteAsync throw a NotSupportedException by default. The synchronous methods of the record reader and writer call Read and Write, and the asynchronous methods call ReadAsync and WriteAsync. Read is called with the field reader at the start of a value record. It may leave fields unread: the record reader skips the rest of the record. Write writes the fields of one record. The record writer ends the record. Header returns the names of the header, or null for no header. A handler is stored in TabularOptions.Handlers or TabularRegistry.Handlers with the record type as the key. One handler instance serves every reader and writer that selects it, on any thread, so a handler must be stateless or thread-safe. The sample writes observations.csv with a handler written by hand for the Observation type: var observations = new Observation[] { new("Kyiv", 50.4501, 30.5234, new(2024, 2, 3), -2.5), new("Ottawa", 45.4215, -75.6972, new(2024, 2, 3), -11.5) }; TabularRegistry.Handlers[typeof(Observation)] = new ObservationHandler(); var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.Create("observations.csv"); using var writer = new TabularWriter<Observation>(stream, dialect); foreach (var observation in observations) { writer.WriteRecord(observation); } internal class ObservationHandler : TabularHandler<Observation> { public override void Write(TabularWriter writer, Observation record) { writer.WriteString(record.City); writer.WriteDouble(record.Latitude); writer.WriteDouble(record.Longitude); writer.WriteDateOnly(record.Date); writer.WriteDouble(record.Temperature); } public override IEnumerable<string?>? Header => ["city", "lat", "lon", "date", "temperature"]; } internal record Observation( string City, double Latitude, double Longitude, DateOnly Date, double Temperature); city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 Arrays as record types An array type can be used as the record type without a handler of its own: the registry has built-in handlers that read a record into an array with one element per field and write an array as a record with one field per element. The length of the array follows the record, so records with different numbers of fields read as arrays of different lengths. These handlers have no header. The supported record types are string?[], Uri?[], and T[] and T?[] for every T of bool, char, Rune, sbyte, byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, Int128, UInt128, BigInteger, Half, BFloat16, float, double, decimal, Decimal32, Decimal64, Decimal128, TimeSpan, DateOnly, TimeOnly, DateTime, DateTimeOffset and Guid. A byte[] record holds one number per field, not base16 or base64 binary data. The elements are read and written with the converter that the reader or writer resolves for the element type, so a converter stored in the options or the registry changes the form of the elements. In string?[], Uri?[] and T?[], an empty field reads as null and a null element is written as an empty field. In T[], an empty field is passed to the converter, which rejects it for most types. A field that cannot be converted throws a TabularException that leaves the reader usable. The sample reads every record of observations.csv, the header included, as an array of five strings: city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.OpenRead("observations.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader<string?[]>(stream, dialect); while (reader.TryReadRecord()) { var observation = reader.CurrentRecord; Console.WriteLine($"{observation[0]}: {observation[4]}"); }

topics/low-level-api.html.summary:
Low-level API TabularReader reads a stream one field at a time, and TabularWriter writes a stream one field at a time. Every member that reads from or writes to the stream has an asynchronous counterpart with a cancellation token, for example TryReadFieldAsync for TryReadField. Invalid arguments and failed conversions throw without changing the state of a reader or writer, so the next call can continue. A failure of the stream itself faults the reader or writer for good: content outside the grammar, which the reader reports with a TabularContentException, a stream or encoding exception, or cancellation. After that, every further operation throws an InvalidOperationException, and a faulted writer discards its buffered text on disposal. Reading fields TryMoveToNextRecord moves to the next record and skips the unread fields of the current one. TryReadField reads the next field of the record and returns false at the end of the record. The samples read and write observations.csv: city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.OpenRead("observations.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader(stream, dialect); reader.TryMoveToNextRecord(); while (reader.TryMoveToNextRecord()) { reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetString(out var observationCity); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetDouble(out var observationLatitude); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetDouble(out var observationLongitude); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetDateOnly(out var observationDate); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetDouble(out var observationTemperature); Console.WriteLine($"{observationCity}: {observationTemperature}"); } CurrentField holds the value of the last read field. It is a region of the reader's buffer, not a copy, and stays valid only until the next call that advances the reader. To keep a field, copy it, for example with TryGetString or CurrentField.ToArray(). TryGetString and the typed accessors (TryGetInt32, TryGetDateTime, …) convert the current field and return false when it does not have the form the type reads, while the Get forms (GetInt32, …) throw a FormatException instead. The typed accessors parse directly from the buffer, without creating a string. TryGet and Get convert with a given converter. The forms of every type are listed in Data types. TrySkipField moves past a field without decoding it, and TryMoveToNextRecord skips the rest of a record the same way, so a reader that needs some fields decodes only those. The sample reads only the cities and temperatures of observations.csv: city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.OpenRead("observations.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader(stream, dialect); reader.TryMoveToNextRecord(); while (reader.TryMoveToNextRecord()) { reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetString(out var observationCity); reader.TrySkipField(); reader.TrySkipField(); reader.TrySkipField(); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetDouble(out var observationTemperature); Console.WriteLine($"{observationCity}: {observationTemperature}"); } Writing fields Each write method appends one field to the current record: WriteString, WriteEmpty, the typed methods (WriteInt32, WriteDateTime, …) and Write with a converter. WriteEndOfRecord ends the record. The sample writes observations.csv: var observations = new (string City, double Latitude, double Longitude, DateOnly Date, double Temperature)[] { new("Kyiv", 50.4501, 30.5234, new(2024, 2, 3), -2.5), new("Ottawa", 45.4215, -75.6972, new(2024, 2, 3), -11.5) }; var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.Create("observations.csv"); using var writer = new TabularWriter(stream, dialect); writer.WriteString("city"); writer.WriteString("lat"); writer.WriteString("lon"); writer.WriteString("date"); writer.WriteString("temperature"); writer.WriteEndOfRecord(); foreach (var observation in observations) { writer.WriteString(observation.City); writer.WriteDouble(observation.Latitude); writer.WriteDouble(observation.Longitude); writer.WriteDateOnly(observation.Date); writer.WriteDouble(observation.Temperature); writer.WriteEndOfRecord(); } city,lat,lon,date,temperature Kyiv,50.4501,30.5234,2024-02-03,-2.5 Ottawa,45.4215,-75.6972,2024-02-03,-11.5 The writer collects text in its buffer and writes a full buffer to the stream without flushing the stream. Only Flush, FlushAsync and disposal flush the stream. Disposal also ends a record that has fields. Readers and writers never close or dispose the stream. Value converters A value converter, a TabularConverter<T>, parses the text of a field into a .NET value and formats a value into text. The typed accessors and write methods of the low-level API and the generated record handlers use the converter that the reader or writer resolves for the type. TabularReader.TryGet, TabularReader.Get and TabularWriter.Write take any converter. A reader or writer resolves the converter for a type the first time it needs it, and keeps it for the rest of its lifetime: The entry for the type in TabularOptions.Converters of the options the reader or writer was created with. Otherwise the entry for the type in TabularRegistry.Converters. Otherwise the call that needs the converter throws an InvalidOperationException. The registry holds the built-in converters for every type in Data types except string and binary data, and is shared by the whole process. The sample stores a date converter with a custom format in the registry, so every reader and writer of the process reads and writes dates in that format, also through TryGetDateOnly and WriteDateOnly: TabularRegistry.Converters[typeof(DateOnly)] = new TabularDateOnlyConverter("dd'.'MM'.'yyyy"); The same converter stored in the options of one reader or writer applies to that reader or writer only. The converters for DateOnly, TimeOnly, DateTime, DateTimeOffset and Guid have a constructor that takes a .NET format string: TabularDateOnlyConverter, TabularTimeOnlyConverter, TabularDateTimeConverter, TabularDateTimeOffsetConverter, TabularGuidConverter. Values are written with the format and read with an exact match of it. The sample reads the dates of observations.csv written as 03.02.2024, passing the converter explicitly: var converter = new TabularDateOnlyConverter("dd'.'MM'.'yyyy"); var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.OpenRead("observations.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader(stream, dialect); reader.TryMoveToNextRecord(); while (reader.TryMoveToNextRecord()) { reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGetString(out var observationCity); reader.TrySkipField(); reader.TrySkipField(); reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGet(converter, out var observationDate); reader.TrySkipField(); Console.WriteLine($"{observationCity}: {observationDate}"); } An attribute of the high-level API names a converter by type, so a custom format there needs a class derived from the converter that passes the format in its public parameterless constructor. A converter in the options or the registry serves every reader and writer that resolves it, and a converter named in a [TabularConverter<T>] attribute is shared by every reader and writer of the record type, on any thread, so a converter must be stateless or immutable. A type without a built-in converter, such as an enumeration, needs a converter of its own. The sample converts the City enumeration by the names of its values and reads the city column of observations.csv as a City value: var converter = new CityConverter(); var dialect = new TabularDialect("
", ',', '"'); using var stream = File.OpenRead("observations.csv"); using var reader = new TabularReader(stream, dialect); reader.TryMoveToNextRecord(); while (reader.TryMoveToNextRecord()) { reader.TryReadField(); reader.TryGet(converter, out var observationCity); Console.WriteLine(observationCity); } internal class CityConverter : TabularConverter<City> { public override bool TryFormat(City value, Span<char> destination, IFormatProvider? provider, out int charsWritten) { return Enum.TryFormat(value, destination, out charsWritten); } public override bool TryParse(ReadOnlySpan<char> source, IFormatProvider? provider, out City value) { return Enum.TryParse(source, out value); } } internal enum City { Kyiv, Ottawa, } The level at which the converter is declared decides where it applies: One call: reader.TryGet(converter, out var city) and writer.Write(city, converter). The readers and writers created with an options instance: options.Converters[typeof(City)] = converter. Every reader and writer of the process: TabularRegistry.Converters[typeof(City)] = converter. One member of a record type: [TabularConverter<CityConverter>]. Every City member of an assembly: [assembly: TabularConverter<CityConverter>].
